q: Take me through the tirage: how much sugar buys how much pressure, and what the yeast must be given to survive a second fermentation in bottle.
accept: about four grams of sugar per litre per atmosphere so 24 g/l for six atmospheres
4 g/l sugar equals one bar plus acclimatised yeast nutrients and a riddling adjuvant
roughly 24 grams per litre of tirage sugar and a slow cool ferment for a fine bead
four grams per atmosphere and the second ferment adds just over one percent alcohol
ans: Roughly 4 grams of sugar per litre yields about one atmosphere of pressure, so a six-atmosphere Champagne takes around 24 g/L in the liqueur de tirage, and that ferment adds a further 1.2–1.3% alcohol on top of the base wine. The yeast cannot be an ordinary strain: it must be acclimatised in a starter culture, alcohol- and pressure-tolerant, pitched at roughly 1.5 million cells per millilitre, and fed with nitrogen and thiamine, because it is being asked to work in a wine already at 11% with no oxygen. A riddling adjuvant — bentonite or alginate — goes in with it so the lees will slide later. The cellar is held near 10–12°C so the fermentation runs slowly over weeks rather than days, which is what gives the finer, more persistent bead.
exp: This single number lets you reason about every sparkling style rather than memorising them: Satèn's five atmospheres, a frizzante's two, a Moscato d'Asti's two-and-a-bit. It also explains why the base wine is picked at modest ripeness — the second fermentation is going to add more than a full percent of alcohol before the wine is even disgorged.

q: Explain autolysis: what physically happens, on what timeline, and what it gives the wine besides flavour.
accept: the yeast die and their enzymes break down the cell walls releasing mannoproteins
enzymatic self-digestion of dead yeast releasing mannoproteins amino acids and maillard aromas
autolysis gives brioche from maillard chemistry and mannoproteins for foam and texture
dead yeast dissolve into the wine improving mousse persistence and mouthfeel
ans: When the second fermentation finishes, the yeast exhaust their sugar and die, and their own enzymes — proteases and glucanases — dismantle the cell walls from the inside, releasing mannoproteins, amino acids, peptides, nucleotides and lipids into the wine. The process starts slowly, is measurable at around twelve months, becomes expressive between 18 months and three years, and continues for decades. The flavour comes largely from Maillard chemistry acting on those released amino acids: bread dough, brioche, toast, hazelnut. But the structural gift is the mannoproteins — they stabilise the foam, so the bead is finer and lasts longer in the glass, they add mid-palate texture, they bind volatile compounds and they help tartrate stability. That is why long-aged traditional-method wine feels creamier, not merely tastes toastier.
exp: Candidates almost always say 'brioche' and stop. The examiner is waiting for mannoproteins and mousse quality. It is also the practical argument for the lees minimums: 9 months for a crémant, 12 months for non-vintage Champagne — inside a 15-month minimum before release — and 30 or 60 months for Franciacorta's millesimato and riserva. Each threshold is chosen against this curve.

q: Lay out Prosecco's hierarchy in full, and explain what Rive and Cartizze mean.
accept: prosecco doc at the base then asolo and conegliano valdobbiadene docg with rive and cartizze
two docgs above the doc rive are named hillsides and cartizze is the grand cru
conegliano valdobbiadene superiore has 43 rive hand harvested and cartizze at the top
asolo and conegliano valdobbiadene are the docgs cartizze about 107 hectares
ans: At the base, Prosecco DOC, spread across nine provinces of the Veneto and Friuli, with Treviso and Trieste as stricter sub-denominations. Above it two DOCGs: Asolo Prosecco, and Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore. Inside the latter sit 43 Rive — named single hillside communes or hamlets, where hand harvesting is compulsory, the vintage must be declared and yields are cut. At the summit, Cartizze: roughly 107 hectares on the steepest slopes above Valdobbiadene, divided among some 140 owners and treated as the grand cru, traditionally finished Dry rather than Brut.
exp: The 2009 reform is the key to all of it: Prosecco stopped being a grape name — the grape was renamed Glera — and became a place, borrowing the village of Prosecco near Trieste so the name could be locked up as a geographical indication. The DOC's sprawl into Friuli, the Rive, the rosé, all of it follows from that single legal manoeuvre.

q: Why does a late-disgorged bottle taste younger than the same base wine disgorged years earlier, and what happens to a bottle in the months after disgorgement?
accept: the lees protect the wine and disgorgement restarts the ageing clock with oxygen pickup
yeast scavenge oxygen so a late disgorged bottle stays fresh then ages faster once opened up
reductive protection on lees ends at disgorgement after which it evolves under cork
the ageing clock resets at disgorgement and the wine needs months to settle afterwards
ans: On the lees the wine is protected. The yeast scavenge oxygen and supply reducing compounds, the crown cap seals tightly, and the wine evolves very slowly along an autolytic rather than an oxidative path. Disgorgement restarts the clock: the wine takes on a slug of dissolved oxygen, loses its reductive buffer, receives its dosage and thereafter ages at the pace of a wine under cork, with slow ingress through the closure. So a bottle of one cuvée disgorged in 2012 will show markedly more tertiary character today than the identical cuvée disgorged last year. In the first months after disgorgement the wine passes through disgorgement shock while the dosage integrates and the sulphur settles — six months is a common rest before release — which is why the disgorgement date on a back label is often more useful than the vintage.
exp: This is the argument for R.D. and late-disgorged bottlings, and the reason to buy on disgorgement date. It also dictates cellar practice: a freshly disgorged bottle wants rest, an old-disgorgement bottle wants drinking.

q: Champagne classifies whole villages rather than individual vineyards. Give the numbers, and explain what that costs the system and what the grower movement did about it.
accept: seventeen grand cru and forty-two premier cru villages of about 319 in total
17 grand crus 42 premier crus out of roughly 319 villages
319 crus with the rating applying to the whole commune not the parcel
grand cru is a whole village rating not a vineyard one which is why lieu-dit bottlings exist
ans: Around 319 crus — villages — of which 17 are rated Grand Cru and 42 Premier Cru; the rest carry no rating. The rating attaches to the entire commune, so a Grand Cru village contains mediocre parcels alongside great ones, and 'Grand Cru' on a Champagne label guarantees only the parish the fruit came from. Burgundy classifies the parcel; Champagne classifies the parish. That gap is precisely what the grower movement exploited, pushing attention down to the lieu-dit and the single parcel — Selosse's Lieux-Dits, Chartogne-Taillet's Les Barres, Krug's Clos du Mesnil — asserting a precision the cru map never encoded.
exp: The trap is assuming this works like Burgundy's classification. It does not, because it rates communes. The ratings descend from the échelle des crus, the percentage scale dating from 1911 that set Grand Cru villages at 100% and Premier Crus at 90–99% and fixed what a grower was paid per kilo — a pricing function that ended with the CIVC's fixed-price mechanism and survives today only as a label term. Say the numbers, say the rating is a parish boundary, then say why single-parcel Champagne exists.
